blocks: GaN Based p-i-n Personal Ultraviolet Photodetection Device
By Derek Shiell, Ryan McClintock, and Alireza Yasan

An ultraviolet UV detection system based on a gallium nitride (GaN) p-i-n ultraviolet (UV) photodetector has been developed to monitor a user’s UV radiation exposure and warn the user before s/he receives a potentially harmful dose of UV radiation. The entire device is portable and consists of a three-stage amplifying circuit, a peripheral interface controller (PIC), a liquid crystal display (LCD), and a GaN based p-i-n UV photodetector. Two buttons allow for user input. The accumulated UV exposure, instantaneous UV exposure, total UV exposure time, skin type, and sun protection factor (SPF) are displayed on an LCD module. It appears possible that this technology could be commercialized, thereby providing a means to reliably prevent UV overexposure and consequently to reduce the incidence of skin cancer among the general population.

Since the 1970’s, the incidence of skin cancer has increased by approximately 3 percent per year.¹ Currently, the number of cases of skin cancer annually is nearly equivalent to all other cases of cancer combined. It is believed that skin cancer is almost exclusively the result of prolonged exposure to ultraviolet (UV) radiation from the sun.² The human body has no way to sense UV radiation directly. Furthermore, excessive exposure results in burning, but by the time burning occurs, the skin has already been damaged. The sun emits an extremely broad spectrum of electromagnetic radiation much of which is absorbed within the ozone layer located in the earth’s upper atmosphere; however, the ozone layer transmits radiation at wavelengths ranging from ~280 nm into the visible region allowing light of these wavelengths to reach the earth’s surface.
Fig. 1 Seasonal irradiance and erythemal weighting function⁹

The light reaching the surface is called the solar irradiance and is about ten times more intense during the summer than during the winter (see Fig. 1). However, the ability of UV radiation to damage the skin is dependent on the wavelength. This leads to an erythemal weighting function, also shown in Figure 1, which can be used to account for the skin’s sensitivity to different wavelengths of light.³ Long exposure to these wavelengths can be harmful to human skin due to the skin’s high sensitivity to UV radiation. Weighting the solar UV irradiance with the erythemal weighting function shows that the greatest potential threat to human skin by UV radiation lies in the region from 280 nm and declines out to 330 nm (Fig. 2).

We have developed a small portable instrument for estimating an individual’s exposure to UV radiation for extended periods of time using a gallium nitride (GaN) based p-i-n UV photodetector. Figure 3 shows the detector structure with the p-type, intrinsic, and n-type layers. The device accounts for the user-specified skin type and sunscreen to warn the user when his/her accumulated exposure to UV radiation reaches potentially harmful levels. The GaN p-i-n photodetector that we have developed for this device detects potentially harmful UV radiation from about 220 nm out to 365 nm, but shows virtually no response outside this range, making it ideal for this application. In addition, the associated electronics and software provide a user-friendly means of operation. It should be noted that numerous other applications exist for UV detectors which cover a wide range of military and industrial uses including: early missile threat detection and interception, chemical and biological threat detection, UV flame monitoring, and industrial UV environmental monitoring.⁴,⁵
